paragraphs: This paper studies reinforcement learning when actions earn rewards while consuming limited resources. The learner initially does not know the transition probabilities, rewards, or resource costs, so it must discover how the system works while managing its remaining budget. The goal is to improve how much experience is needed to learn effective constrained decisions.

The method repeatedly solves a linear programming formulation of the decision problem, updating resource capacities as learning proceeds. Its analysis identifies problem difficulty through the structure of an optimal linear programming basis. An elimination procedure finds one such basis, and subsequent optimization uses that structure while adapting to the resources still available.

The authors derive logarithmic regret and a sample bound proportional to log²(1/ε)/(Δε), where ε measures the desired accuracy and Δ depends on the problem rather than ε. This improves the dependence on accuracy over earlier 1/ε² bounds. The result is explicitly problem dependent: its significance is the sharper accuracy scaling together with an analysis connecting learning difficulty to optimization structure.
neurips-2024-achieving-tilde-o-1-epsilon.tldr: An adaptive linear programming approach improves constrained reinforcement learning’s accuracy dependence to roughly 1/ε, with an additional problem-dependent factor.

paragraphs: Calcium imaging can record activity from enormous numbers of neurons, but processing those recordings still involves substantial human judgment. Automated extraction produces candidate cells and activity traces, including false positives that researchers must remove. ActSort addresses this curation step, called cell sorting, which becomes increasingly burdensome as recordings grow.

The algorithm uses active learning to decide which candidates deserve human annotation. It brings unusual candidates near its decision boundary to the annotator, concentrating effort on examples that can clarify uncertain classifications. The system combines features designed by domain experts with data representations that require little memory, addressing both annotation effort and the practical size of these datasets.

The authors report reducing human annotation to about 1–3% of cell candidates while improving curation accuracy through reduced annotator bias. They also provide user-friendly software and evaluate it in a study containing about 160,000 annotations across experimental conditions and multiple animals. These findings support ActSort as a way to relieve a major processing bottleneck in large-scale neural recording experiments.
neurips-2024-actsort-an-active-learning-.tldr: ActSort targets informative cell candidates for human review, reducing annotation effort while improving curation of large calcium imaging datasets.

paragraphs: Video models are commonly evaluated on activities and settings centered on humans. That leaves their ability to understand animals less thoroughly tested, despite potential relevance to animal welfare and conservation. Animal-Bench provides an evaluation framework organized around animals, broadening the kinds of subjects and tasks used to assess multimodal video understanding.

The benchmark contains 13 tasks across seven major animal categories and 819 species, totaling 41,839 data entries. Some tasks overlap with familiar human-centered evaluations, while others address animal conservation. The authors define an animal-centered task system and build an automated data-processing pipeline, giving the benchmark a structured basis beyond simply collecting animal videos.

The evaluation also includes edited videos that simulate challenges such as changing weather and shooting conditions associated with animal movement. Tests of eight multimodal video models reveal considerable room for improvement. The contribution is therefore both a broader test collection and evidence that existing models still face substantial challenges on animal-focused tasks, including robustness under the simulated viewing conditions.
neurips-2024-animal-bench-benchmarking-m.tldr: Animal-Bench evaluates video models across diverse animal tasks and species, revealing substantial room for improvement.

paragraphs: Human collaborators can change their initiative and strategy during a shared task. An AI partner therefore faces a moving target: behavior that worked with one collaboration style may become less suitable when the person changes approach. This paper argues that representing the final collaborative agent with a single policy network is insufficient for handling these changing dynamics.

Collaborative Bayesian Policy Reuse, or CBPR, draws on the observation that different human behaviors can involve similar underlying meta-tasks. It trains agents for those meta-tasks and uses Bayesian reasoning to select among multiple policy networks as collaboration unfolds. Adaptation thus includes choosing an appropriate collaborative policy, rather than relying entirely on action selection within one network.

The authors provide theoretical guarantees for rapid convergence to the optimal policy after a human partner changes policies. Experiments and user studies in the Overcooked cooking simulator show stronger performance than the evaluated baselines. Together, these results support organizing collaborative expertise around recurring meta-tasks as a useful approach to partners whose behavior changes over time.
neurips-2024-beyond-single-stationary-po.tldr: CBPR adapts to changing human partners by selecting among policies trained for recurring collaborative meta-tasks.

paragraphs: Softmax attention captures relationships across an image but becomes computationally expensive at high resolution. Linear attention offers more favorable computational scaling, yet its weaker performance has limited adoption. This paper investigates the reasons for that gap and identifies two properties that help explain why the approaches behave differently.

The first is injectivity: whether different query vectors can be distinguished by the attention operation. The authors prove that linear attention is not injective, meaning distinct queries can receive identical attention weights and produce the same outputs. This can confuse different semantic requests. The second property is local modeling, or effectively representing nearby visual information, which the authors identify as essential to Softmax attention’s success and weaker in linear attention.

Extensive experiments support the importance of both properties. Further results show that linear attention equipped with them can outperform Softmax attention across various tasks while retaining lower computational complexity. The findings connect an efficiency–performance tradeoff to specific representational weaknesses and show empirically that addressing those weaknesses can improve the tradeoff.
neurips-2024-bridging-the-divide-reconsi.tldr: Preserving query distinctions and strengthening local modeling can help linear attention outperform Softmax attention while retaining lower computational complexity.

paragraphs: Cross-domain segmentation often learns from pseudo-labels: predictions treated as training labels on new data. Under substantial domain shifts, even supposedly reliable pixels can form scattered, incorrect predictions. Unfamiliar classes can also receive high confidence. Repeated training on these mistakes allows errors to accumulate, making confidence-based selection of individual pixels problematic.

Semantic Connectivity-driven Pseudo-labeling, or SeCo, organizes predictions into connected semantic regions. Its Pixel Semantic Aggregation component separates semantics into stuff and things categories and interacts with the Segment Anything Model to assemble scattered labels into regions with accurate boundaries. This organization makes erroneous labels easier to locate at a meaningful spatial scale.

A second component, Semantic Connectivity Correction, uses a region classification task and its loss distribution to locate and correct noisy regions. Experiments show improvements when SeCo is applied to domain generalization and several forms of domain adaptation, including source-free and black-box settings. The central finding is that connected structure provides useful evidence for correcting both known-class mistakes and noise involving unfamiliar classes.
neurips-2024-connectivity-driven-pseudo-.tldr: SeCo improves cross-domain segmentation by grouping pseudo-labels into connected regions and correcting noise at that level.

paragraphs: In predict-then-optimize systems, a model makes predictions that feed into a downstream decision procedure. Prediction quality matters through the decisions it produces, motivating training losses that reflect decision outcomes. This paper introduces Perturbation Gradient losses, a family of surrogate objectives that directly approximate downstream decision loss and support standard gradient-based optimization.

The key theoretical property is that their approximation error vanishes as the sample count increases. Consequently, optimizing these losses yields an asymptotically best policy within the chosen model class, even when that class cannot represent the underlying relationship exactly. This qualification matters: best-in-class performance concerns the available models, while misspecification means the true relationship may lie outside that class.

Numerical results show substantial improvements over existing proposals when the model is misspecified and the noise is not centrally symmetric. The approach is particularly relevant when a simpler or more interpretable model is desirable despite imperfect fit. It connects computationally tractable training with a guarantee about eventual decision quality, rather than only about the accuracy of intermediate predictions.
neurips-2024-decision-focused-learning-w.tldr: Perturbation Gradient losses support gradient-based decision-aware training with asymptotic best-in-class guarantees even under model misspecification.

paragraphs: Federated learning systems can have several aggregation levels, with clients organized into groups before their updates reach a global model. Different datasets can cause individual clients to drift away from their group’s direction, while groups also drift away from the global direction. These effects occur across multiple update timescales, complicating training in hierarchical systems.

Multi-Timescale Gradient Correction addresses the two sources of drift with separate control variables. One corrects client gradients toward the group gradient. Another corrects group gradients toward the global gradient. This design explicitly accounts for the hierarchy instead of treating data differences as a single source of disagreement.

The authors analyze convergence for general non-convex objectives while handling interactions between the correction terms. Their convergence bound does not depend on the extent of data heterogeneity, providing theoretical support for stability across differing client and group datasets. Experiments on multiple datasets and models also support the method’s effectiveness. The contribution combines a correction mechanism matched to the system structure with an analysis of how its coupled updates converge.
neurips-2024-hierarchical-federated-lear.tldr: Separate corrections for client and group gradients stabilize hierarchical federated learning, with a convergence bound independent of data heterogeneity.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning should be able to use value estimates to learn from data that is less than expert quality. Yet it often underperforms imitation learning, raising a question about where the learning pipeline breaks down. This paper separately examines value learning, extracting a policy from learned values, and generalizing that policy to states encountered during testing.

The empirical study finds that policy extraction often affects performance and scalability more than the value-learning objective. Common value-weighted behavioral cloning methods do not fully use the learned value function. Switching to behavior-constrained policy gradient objectives often produces substantial improvements, showing that how values influence action choices can be a major bottleneck.

The study also identifies weak policy generalization to states outside the training data’s support as an important barrier. Data with broader coverage can help even when its behavior is suboptimal. The authors additionally propose two test-time policy improvement methods and report better performance. These findings shift attention toward extracting useful behavior and adapting it to unfamiliar states, alongside improving value estimates.
neurips-2024-is-value-learning-really-th.tldr: An empirical study finds that policy extraction and generalization often constrain offline reinforcement learning more than value learning does.

paragraphs: Entity alignment seeks corresponding entities across knowledge graphs, but some entities have no counterpart. These dangling cases become particularly relevant when graphs differ in scale. The paper studies a setting where matched pairs are labeled while dangling entities remain unlabeled, reflecting the lower cost of collecting known matches compared with identifying entities that cannot be matched.

Lambda combines entity alignment with dangling detection. Its graph neural network encoder, KEESA, learns representations using a spectral contrastive objective for alignment. Its iPULE component uses positive-unlabeled learning to identify dangling cases. This separates learning what corresponds across graphs from deciding whether a counterpart exists at all.

The dangling detection method has theoretical guarantees covering unbiasedness, uniform deviation bounds, and convergence. Experiments show that both components contribute to performance and that Lambda surpasses the evaluated baselines even when those baselines additionally receive labels for 30% of dangling entities. The results support jointly addressing correspondence and matchability when annotation provides positive matches but does not explicitly identify all unmatched cases.
neurips-2024-lambda-learning-matchable-p.tldr: Lambda combines graph-based alignment and positive-unlabeled learning to match entities while detecting those with no counterpart.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether gradient flow can learn a high-dimensional target using a model with fewer parameters than target dimensions. Its main theorem gives a striking possibility result: for targets described by a particular probability distribution, suitably constructed models with only two parameters can achieve arbitrarily high probability of successful learning.

That probabilistic result coexists with strong geometric restrictions. Whenever the parameter count is below the target dimension, there must be a large collection of targets that gradient flow cannot learn. The learnable set is not dense in the full target space. Furthermore, every subset shaped topologically like a sphere of the parameter dimension contains targets that cannot be learned.

The successful two-parameter model relies on a hierarchical construction and cannot be expressed as a single elementary function. The authors show that this feature is essential: most models expressed through elementary functions cannot attain the theorem’s learnability. The findings therefore distinguish distribution-specific, high-probability success from broad coverage of target space, while showing that parameter count alone does not capture every theoretical learning possibility.
neurips-2024-learnability-of-high-dimens.tldr: Specially constructed two-parameter models can learn high-dimensional targets with high probability, despite unavoidable geometric and representational limits.

paragraphs: Some statistical signals appear in relationships among several variables rather than simple pairwise correlations. This paper studies such information through a spiked cumulant model, where a hidden direction is encoded in cumulants of order four or higher. The authors investigate the data requirements for distinguishing these inputs from isotropic Gaussian data.

An exact likelihood-ratio norm formula sharpens the distinction between statistical possibility and efficient computation. Statistical distinguishability requires at least order d samples, where d is input dimension. For the broad algorithmic class covered by the low-degree conjecture, polynomial-time distinguishability requires at least order d² samples. The computational conclusion is tied to that conjectural framework and algorithmic scope.

Numerical experiments show neural networks learning to distinguish the distributions with quadratic sample complexity. Random-feature methods, representing a lazy-learning approach, perform no better than chance in that regime. Within this model, the results indicate that neural networks can efficiently extract higher-order information and reveal a substantial difference in the data needed by neural networks and random features.
neurips-2024-learning-from-higher-order-.tldr: In a spiked cumulant model, neural networks empirically learn higher-order signals with quadratic sample complexity where random features fail.

paragraphs: DNA, RNA, and proteins provide related views of biological information, but many pretrained sequence models handle only one of these modalities. Problems involving relationships between them require a way to combine their learned representations. This paper introduces IsoFormer, a multimodal model built from pretrained encoders specialized for the different sequence types.

The application focuses on transcript isoforms: different RNA transcripts originating from the same gene. These transcripts can have different expression levels across human tissues, so the shared DNA sequence alone does not describe all relevant variation. IsoFormer combines information from DNA, RNA, and protein encoders to predict differential transcript expression.

The authors report accurate expression predictions that outperform existing methods and benefit from using multiple modalities. They also find efficient transfer of knowledge from encoder pretraining and between modalities. The contribution is a framework for connecting existing biological sequence models on a problem that intrinsically spans their individual scopes. Its open-source release makes that combined modeling approach available for further work on multimodal gene expression.
neurips-2024-multi-modal-transfer-learni.tldr: IsoFormer combines pretrained DNA, RNA, and protein encoders to improve prediction of transcript expression across human tissues.

paragraphs: Offline safe reinforcement learning trains decision policies from previously collected data while seeking to satisfy safety constraints. A central difficulty is that the available demonstrations may not exhibit the combination of safety and reward the learner needs. OASIS addresses this mismatch by changing the training data distribution toward a more useful target.

The method uses a conditional diffusion model to synthesize offline datasets. This provides a way to shape the examples available for learning, rather than accepting the original demonstrations as the only training distribution. Data utilization and regularization techniques support learning behavior that complies with constraints while pursuing reward.

Evaluations on public benchmarks and varied datasets show that OASIS helps offline agents achieve high reward while satisfying safety constraints, outperforming the tested baselines. The authors also report strong data efficiency and robustness. These findings support data distribution shaping as a useful approach when high-quality demonstrations are scarce, with potential relevance to safety-critical applications. The stated evidence concerns performance in the evaluated settings rather than a universal guarantee for deployment.
neurips-2024-oasis-conditional-distribut.tldr: OASIS synthesizes training data with a conditional diffusion model to improve reward and constraint satisfaction in offline safe reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: Few-shot anomaly detection must identify unusual image content using only a small number of normal examples. Recent methods use pretrained vision-language models, but directly comparing a query image’s features with those few examples can reduce precision. The paper proposes making the normal reference more specific to the query being examined.

Its anomaly personalization method transforms each query into a customized anomaly-free version using a generation model. This one-to-normal transformation aims to align the result closely with normal data, creating a reference tailored to the individual image. A triplet contrastive inference strategy then compares the query with a generated anomaly-free data pool and prompt information to improve prediction stability and robustness.

Evaluations cover eleven datasets across three domains and show effectiveness relative to recent anomaly detection methods. The authors also demonstrate that the generated images can improve other anomaly detectors. The findings suggest that producing relevant normal reference data can help both the proposed inference method and existing systems, extending the usefulness of personalization beyond a single detector.
neurips-2024-one-to-normal-anomaly-perso.tldr: Generating a personalized anomaly-free reference for each query improves few-shot anomaly detection and can benefit other detectors.

paragraphs: Online paging decides which pages to retain in a cache as requests arrive. In weighted paging, fetching different pages incurs different costs, making eviction decisions depend on more than whether a page is currently stored. Previous work assumes those costs are known, but practical fetching costs may depend on uncertain conditions such as availability in intermediate cache levels.

The paper introduces an algorithm that learns page weights from samples of fetching costs while making online caching decisions. This brings cost estimation into the paging problem itself. Repeated observations provide information that is unavailable in advance, allowing the algorithm to work with unknown weights rather than requiring them as inputs.

The technical challenge is connecting discrete samples to a fractional optimization solver, whose decisions must then be converted into actual cache choices through randomized rounding. The authors develop a careful interface between those pieces. The contribution extends weighted paging to learned costs; the cited optimal logarithmic competitive bound belongs to earlier work with known weights, not a stated bound for the new algorithm.
neurips-2024-online-weighted-paging-with.tldr: A new online paging algorithm learns unknown fetching costs from samples while coordinating fractional optimization with discrete cache decisions.

paragraphs: Simulation offers inexpensive experience for reinforcement learning, but a policy trained there may fail when deployed in the real world. This paper investigates whether a simulator can still help in those cases. Its central idea is to transfer policies that support exploration, giving the real-world learner useful ways to gather information.

The authors show that, in many regimes where direct policy transfer fails, simulation can produce a useful collection of exploratory policies. In low-rank Markov decision processes, combining these policies with least-squares regression and randomized exploration yields polynomial real-world sample complexity. In the studied setting, this is an exponential improvement over direct transfer or learning without a simulator.

Experiments in several realistic robotic simulators and a real-world robotic task also show substantial practical gains from transferring exploration policies. The theoretical result depends on the low-rank setting, while the experiments provide complementary evidence of practical usefulness. Together, they show how simulation can contribute to learning after transfer even when its policy does not immediately perform the intended task successfully.
neurips-2024-overcoming-the-sim-to-real-.tldr: Simulation-trained exploration policies can accelerate real-world learning even when directly transferring a task policy fails.

paragraphs: PeRFlow accelerates diffusion models by changing the paths followed during generation. The method treats sampling as a flow evolving over time and divides that evolution into several windows. Within each window, it applies a reflow operation that straightens the trajectory, making the overall process approach a sequence of linear path segments.

This piecewise structure is central to the approach: each interval is simplified locally, yielding a flow suited to generation with few sampling steps. The authors report superior performance in that few-step setting. The method therefore links acceleration to the geometry of the sampling trajectory, with the individual time windows providing the units of simplification.

PeRFlow also uses parameterizations that preserve knowledge from pretrained diffusion models. The authors report fast training convergence and favorable transfer ability, allowing the resulting models to act as plug-and-play accelerators across various workflows built on those pretrained models. The contribution combines a way to simplify sampling with a way to retain useful pretrained behavior, supporting acceleration across multiple existing generation workflows.
neurips-2024-perflow-piecewise-rectified.tldr: PeRFlow speeds diffusion generation by straightening sampling trajectories within time windows while retaining pretrained model knowledge.

paragraphs: This paper studies replicable learning through partitions of geometric space. A secluded partition limits how many regions a small neighborhood can intersect. That limit, k, is connected to a learner’s list complexity, while the neighborhood radius, ε, is connected to sample complexity. Desirable partitions support a larger radius while keeping the number of intersected regions small.

The authors prove restrictions on this tradeoff when each region has at most unit measure. In d dimensions, k must be at least (1 + 2ε)^d. They also construct partitions into unit cubes that approach the resulting radius bound within a logarithmic factor in dimension. These matching directions establish a near-optimal relationship between the geometric parameters.

The proof techniques additionally yield a neighborhood version of the cubical KKM-Sperner lemma. Under a coloring rule that forbids sharing colors across opposing faces, some small neighborhood must intersect many colors, with an exponential dependence on dimension for fixed radius. The results sharpen both constructions and impossibility arguments relevant to replicable learning.
neurips-2024-replicability-in-learning-g.tldr: Near-optimal bounds on geometric partitions clarify tradeoffs relevant to replicable learning and yield a neighborhood version of the KKM-Sperner lemma.

paragraphs: TabularBench addresses the limited standardization of adversarial robustness evaluation for deep learning on tables. The authors hypothesize that this gap has slowed research on attacks and defenses compared with computer vision. Their benchmark creates a shared setting for assessing how tabular classifiers respond to evasion attacks and how defensive training changes that response.

The evaluation uses CAA, an ensemble combining gradient-based and search-based attacks. It covers more than 200 models across five scenarios in finance, healthcare, and security. The authors implement seven robustness mechanisms inspired by vision defenses and curate real datasets supplemented with hundreds of thousands of realistic synthetic inputs. Models are trained and evaluated both with and without data augmentation.

The project releases a benchmark and a library providing access to pretrained robust models and the real and synthetic datasets. Its analysis examines the impact of defenses and offers guidance for developing new ones. The contribution is a common experimental foundation for comparing robustness strategies across practical tabular tasks, rather than a claim that one defense solves every scenario.
neurips-2024-tabularbench-benchmarking-a.tldr: TabularBench provides shared datasets, attacks, defenses, and pretrained models for evaluating adversarial robustness in tabular deep learning.

paragraphs: This paper asks when a well-observed source network can help estimate a sparsely observed target network. The quantity to recover is the target’s matrix of edge probabilities conditional on latent variables. Available data includes source-network edges and target edges only within a subgraph containing a fraction of nodes that tends to zero.

If the networks are unrelated, estimation error must remain bounded away from zero. The authors show that shared latent variables can make vanishing error possible. Their efficient algorithm uses the ordering induced by a suitably defined graph distance and achieves error tending to zero without specifying a parametric form for either network.

For stochastic block models, the paper further establishes a minimax lower bound and gives a simple algorithm attaining that rate. Experiments on simulated and real graph transfer problems illustrate the approach. The central message is that shared hidden structure can make extremely limited target observations useful, while the lack of any source–target relationship prevents the same estimation conclusion.
neurips-2024-transfer-learning-for-laten.tldr: Shared latent variables can enable accurate target-network estimation from a fully observed source and a vanishing fraction of target nodes.

paragraphs: Combining task-specialized models can produce a multitask model, but their knowledge may interfere when merged. A fixed combination can also struggle with test inputs that vary substantially. This paper finds that both shared and task-exclusive knowledge matter, while directly merging exclusive knowledge can hurt overall performance.

Twin-Merging first separates knowledge into shared and exclusive components, then compresses them to reduce redundancy. At inference, it combines shared and task-specific knowledge dynamically according to the input. This gives the merging process a way to preserve specialized information while adjusting which expertise contributes to each prediction.

Experiments cover 20 datasets spanning language and vision. The authors report an average improvement of 28.34% in absolute normalized score on discriminative tasks and performance exceeding the fine-tuned reference described as an upper bound on generative tasks. These are results from the evaluated tasks, supporting the method’s ability to narrow the gap with specialized models and adapt to heterogeneous inputs. The findings emphasize retaining modular expertise and selecting its contribution dynamically.
neurips-2024-twin-merging-dynamic-integr.tldr: Twin-Merging separates shared and specialized knowledge, then combines it according to each input to improve merged-model performance.

paragraphs: Randomly sampling data before applying a differentially private mechanism can strengthen privacy guarantees. Conventional analyses summarize this improvement using only the original mechanism’s privacy parameters. This paper develops a general framework that also uses information about the mechanism itself, allowing a tighter characterization of privacy after subsampling.

The framework is based on conditional optimal transport and unifies several forms of privacy analysis. It derives both existing and new guarantees for approximate differential privacy, Rényi differential privacy accounting, and accounting with dominating pairs. This matters for iterative training because privacy accounting tracks the accumulated privacy cost across many applications of a mechanism.

As an application, the authors examine privacy for groups of multiple users under subsampling. Their tight mechanism-specific bounds improve on tight mechanism-agnostic bounds and classic group privacy results. The gain comes from incorporating additional mechanism information into the analysis. The contribution therefore provides a common mathematical route to sharper privacy accounting, including cases where protection must be assessed for more than one user together.
neurips-2024-unified-mechanism-specific-.tldr: A conditional optimal transport framework uses mechanism-specific information to tighten subsampling and group privacy guarantees.

paragraphs: Image segmentation models learn to assign meaningful categories or regions to pixels, raising concerns when training uses private images without authorization. UnSeg explores protection through unlearnable examples: images modified with noise intended to disrupt their usefulness for training. The aim is a reusable generator that can apply this transformation to downstream images.

The generator is fine-tuned from the Segment Anything Model using an interactive segmentation dataset. Training uses bilevel optimization and a surrogate segmentation model that shares SAM’s architecture but starts from scratch. The optimization seeks to minimize that surrogate’s training error while learning the noise generator, producing the image modifications used by the protection framework.

The authors evaluate UnSeg across six segmentation tasks, ten datasets, and seven network architectures. They report large reductions in segmentation performance when models train on the modified images. These experiments support the generator’s transfer across the tested settings, with the broader contribution showing how a foundation model can support data-efficient and computationally affordable image protection. The empirical breadth supports versatility without establishing effectiveness against every possible segmentation system.
neurips-2024-unseg-one-universal-unlearn.tldr: UnSeg adapts SAM into a reusable noise generator that substantially degrades segmentation learning from protected images across tested settings.

paragraphs: Concept bottleneck models make predictions through intermediate concepts intended to be understandable to people. But an explanation becomes questionable if those concepts do not match the image. Concept values can also carry unintended information, allowing strong classification even when the named concepts themselves provide little meaningful explanation.

VLG-CBM addresses these issues with visually grounded concept annotations from existing open-domain grounded object detectors. These annotations connect concept learning more closely to visible image content. The authors also introduce Number of Effective Concepts, or NEC, a metric intended to control information leakage and support more interpretable evaluation.

Across five benchmarks, VLG-CBM improves the reported Accuracy at NEC=5 measure by 4.27% to 51.09% over existing methods, and the average-accuracy measure by 0.45% to 29.78%. Experiments also support the faithfulness and interpretability of its learned concepts. The contribution links improved prediction with stronger grounding of the explanatory layer, while using concept-sensitive evaluation to examine whether predictive success corresponds to useful, understandable intermediate representations.
neurips-2024-vlg-cbm-training-concept-bo.tldr: VLG-CBM uses visually grounded concept annotations and concept-sensitive evaluation to improve accuracy and faithful interpretation.
